mcqs.question: A model's uptime, error rate, and latency dashboards all look completely healthy, yet its predictions have become steadily less accurate over the past three months. Why don't standard application monitoring tools catch this?
options: Because the model server must be crashing intermittently, which the dashboards are failing to record
Because this type of degradation is actually impossible for a well-trained model
Because latency monitoring is the correct tool for detecting this, and the team must have misconfigured it

Because model quality degradation from a changing world produces no errors or exceptions — the model keeps returning confident, well-formed predictions that are simply increasingly wrong, a failure mode standard infra monitoring isn't designed to detect
mcqs.explanation: This is the defining characteristic of silent model degradation: predictions remain syntactically valid and confidently returned even as the world diverges from the training distribution, so uptime/error-rate/latency monitoring — designed to catch crashes and slow responses — has nothing to flag. There's no implied crash here (A is inconsistent with "all dashboards look healthy"), latency monitoring isn't designed to catch prediction-quality drift regardless of configuration (C is false), and this degradation is a well-documented, common failure mode, not impossible (D is false).

mcqs.question: A fraud-detection model's accuracy drops because fraudsters have adopted a new tactic that mimics previously-legitimate transaction patterns. Is this data drift or concept drift, and why does the distinction matter?
options: Concept drift, because the relationship between features and the true label changed — the same feature pattern now means something different — which generally requires retraining on newly labeled data reflecting the new relationship, not just better feature coverage
Data drift, because the input feature distribution changed
Neither term applies; this is simply normal model variance
Data drift and concept drift are interchangeable terms for the same phenomenon
mcqs.explanation: This is concept drift specifically: the feature values (transaction patterns) may look similar to before, but what those patterns now indicate (fraud vs legitimate) has changed, meaning the fundamental mapping the model learned is now wrong — the fix requires retraining on data that reflects the new fraud-legitimate relationship, not just adjusting for a changed input distribution. It isn't data drift, since the issue isn't primarily about input distribution shift but about the label relationship (A is a common but incorrect conflation), this isn't normal variance — it's a systematic distribution/relationship shift (C is false), and the two terms describe genuinely distinct phenomena with different fixes (D is false).

mcqs.question: Why is monitoring input feature distributions typically the very first alerting layer set up for a production model, ahead of monitoring predictions or business outcomes?
options: Because feature distribution monitoring is more accurate than any other monitoring layer
Because feature distributions require no ground-truth labels and can be computed the instant a request comes in, making them the earliest and cheapest available drift signal
Because business metrics can only be computed after feature monitoring is fully set up
Because prediction distributions cannot be computed without labeled data
mcqs.explanation: Feature-distribution monitoring's advantage is timing, not superior accuracy: it needs zero ground-truth labels, so it can flag a shift the moment a request arrives, well before enough new labeled data exists to detect an accuracy change directly — that's exactly why it's usually the first monitoring layer built. It isn't claimed to be more "accurate" than other layers (B), there's no dependency requiring feature monitoring before business-metric monitoring can be built (C is false), and prediction distributions are also computable without labels (D is false — that's precisely why prediction monitoring is another label-free layer).

mcqs.question: A recommendation model's click-through rate on delivered recommendations stays statistically stable, but company revenue from recommended purchases drops noticeably over the same period. What does this suggest about relying on prediction-distribution monitoring alone?
options: It confirms prediction-distribution monitoring is always sufficient on its own
This scenario is impossible if click-through rate is stable

It shows why downstream business-metric monitoring is still necessary — a model can appear stable by its own prediction statistics (click-through) while still failing the actual business goal (revenue) it's meant to serve
Revenue drops are always caused by factors completely unrelated to the model
mcqs.explanation: This is exactly the gap between prediction monitoring and business-outcome monitoring: the model's own output statistics can look fine (people are still clicking recommendations at the usual rate) while the ultimate metric the system exists to serve — revenue — quietly degrades, perhaps because clicked items convert to purchases less often. This directly contradicts treating prediction monitoring alone as sufficient (A is false), the scenario described is realistic, not impossible (C is false), and while other factors could contribute, dismissing the model's role outright (D) ignores that this is precisely the failure mode the topic describes monitoring for.

mcqs.question: A team relies solely on monthly scheduled retraining for a model in a fast-moving adversarial domain (fraud), where tactics can shift meaningfully within days. What is the main risk of this choice?
options: Scheduled retraining is always superior to drift-triggered retraining regardless of domain
This approach has no meaningful downside as long as the model was accurate at launch
Monthly retraining is technically impossible to implement

A month-long gap between retrains means a fast-moving concept drift can cause real, ongoing harm for weeks before the next scheduled update catches it — drift-triggered retraining (or a combination with scheduled retraining) reacts faster to this kind of shift
mcqs.explanation: The core risk of pure scheduled retraining in an adversarial, fast-moving domain is the lag between when drift starts and when the next scheduled retrain happens — in fraud specifically, that gap can mean weeks of degraded detection before the fix arrives, which is why combining scheduled retraining with drift-triggered retraining is common in exactly this kind of domain. Scheduled retraining isn't universally superior (A is false — the topic explicitly notes its weakness in fast-moving cases), monthly retraining is a perfectly implementable approach (C is false), and the risk described is real and significant, not negligible (D is false).

mcqs.question: A team building a loan-default model plans to monitor solely via live accuracy, waiting for ground-truth default outcomes to arrive. What is the fundamental problem with this plan?
options: Loan-default outcomes may not be knowable for up to a year, meaning an accuracy-only monitoring strategy would always be looking backward at stale information, or provide no timely signal at all
Accuracy is impossible to compute for any classification model
This plan works fine, since default outcomes are always known within a day
Live accuracy monitoring requires no ground-truth labels at all, so this concern doesn't apply
mcqs.explanation: This is precisely the pitfall the topic warns about: for a loan-default model, the true label (did the borrower actually default?) may only become known up to a year later, so relying solely on accuracy means the monitoring signal is always dangerously delayed relative to when a real problem might be occurring — label-free signals (feature and prediction distribution monitoring) are what fill this gap. Accuracy is computable, just not promptly here (B is false), default outcomes for a loan product are realistically not known within a day (C is false), and accuracy by definition requires ground-truth labels, which is exactly the source of the delay problem (D is false).
